world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.source_named: MacKinlay, W. E. W. 1905. A Handbook and Grammar of the Tagalog Language. Washington: GPO, Accents section (archive.org full text, read). Filipino = standardized Tagalog.
earlier_scan.note: Contrastive lexical stress, typically final or penultimate; minimal pairs distinguished by accent alone.

new_statements.quote: The great majority of words in Filipino fall into two classes: penult-prominent and ultima-prominent. [...] There are loanwords with antepenultimate prominence, such as [ʔágila] 'eagle', from Spanish águila [...] And there are loans with prominence on a closed penult, such as [bɾiljánte] 'diamond', from Spanish brillante. [...] All this is evidence in favour of analysing Filipino as having stress, even though the stress is realised differently in different positions in speech, with stressed penults having greater duration than unstressed, and stressed ultimas having greater loudness than unstressed (in addition to possible intonational differences).
new_statements.citation: Zuraw, Kie & Paolo Roca. 2025. Evidence for stress in Filipino text-setting. Phonology 42:e7, 1-30. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0952675725000041 (Open Access CC-BY)

All three quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: §2.2.1 lines 146-147 (p. 3) 'The great majority of words in Filipino fall into two classes: penult-prominent and ultima-prominent.'; p. 4 lines 196-200 'There are loanwords with antepenultimate prominence, such as [ʔágila] 'eagle', from Spanish águila, which was the only such word in the song corpus we used. And there are loans with prominence on a closed penult, such as [bɾiljánte] 'diamond', from S…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is lexically contrastive between the penult and the ultima (minimal pairs [ʔábot] 'power' vs [ʔabót] 'arrival'); it is not predictable from the word's shape except that a closed penult cannot bear stress (so words with a closed penult are final-stressed, cf. Bloomfield 1917 §39, Blake 1925 §13c) and that stress must fall within the last two syllables (Blake 1925 §12: 'regularly on one of the last two syllables, but there is no rule for determining in all cases on which of these two syllables it falls'). Loanwords may have antepenult stress (ʔágila) or stress on a closed penult (bɾiljánte, kwénto). Under suffixation (verbal -in/-an) stress shifts one syllable to the right, staying penult or final respectively (súlat -> sulátin, dasál -> dasalín); some noun derivations change the pattern idiosyncratically. Penult stress is cued mainly by vowel length, final stress mainly by loudness; scholars are split between a phonemic-length analysis (Schachter & Otanes 1972; Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020) and a phonemic-stress analysis (Bloomfield 1917; Blake 1925; French 1988, 1991), and Zuraw & Roca argue for the latter.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, described by all primary sources. Bloomfield 1917 §§43-44: secondary accents on aspect reduplicants and other pre-tonic syllables (sùsúlat 'will write', nàràramdamàn), with vowel lengthening up to twice an unstressed vowel; Blake 1925 §16: 'Words of more than two syllables with ultimate accent, and those of more than three syllables with penultimate accent, have a secondary stress on the second syllable before the principal stress' (kàniyá, dàlitá); French 1988/1991 (via Zuraw & Roca §8.1, p. 20): aspect reduplicants and closed prefix syllables attract secondary stress ([ˌsuˈsulat], [màg-pa-ka-ʔáɾal]); Zuraw & Roca's text-setting data (§8, pp. 20-23) support secondary stress on pre-tonic long-vowel and closed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Closed penult cannot be stressed except in loans (bɾiljánte, kwénto) and a few native items (mínsan, pínsan, -ay syllables per Bloomfield §39); a few Spanish loans have antepenult stress (ʔágila); monosyllabic function words and atonic particles (ang, at, ay, sa, si, ng, na) are unstressed (Bloomfield §45); when an ultima-stressed word is followed by a phrase-final enclitic the intonational pitch accent moves to the enclitic (damít ko) though the text-setting data still treat mít as the prominent syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, lexical words (mostly disyllabic roots plus affixed derivatives); Zuraw & Roca's Table 1 (p. 3) separates citation-form pitch accent from behaviour in longer phrases, where the phrase-final pitch accent may move onto a final word or clitic (Schachter & Otanes 1972: 32 'fixed-P2 patterns'). Bloomfield 1917 §§45-46 separately treats sentence accent (atonic words, loss of final-syllable accent before a following word in close phrases).
new_statements.identity_note: Filipino (fili1244, ISO fil) is the standardized national variety of Tagalog (taga1270, ISO tgl); Zuraw & Roca 2025 explicitly use 'Filipino' (national-media language, OPM corpus) while noting all their linguistic sources say 'Tagalog', and they treat the two as one system for word prosody. All the older first-hand grammars downloaded (Bloomfield 1917 Manila Tagalog; Blake 1925; MacKinlay 1905; Lendoyro 1909) describe Tagalog; the same files serve taga1270, where a copy of Zuraw & Roca already sits. Dialectal Tagalog (e.g. Marinduque, Soberano 1980) is not covered.

new_statements.quote: This, in conjunction with the divergent behavior of penultimate and final prominence, strongly suggests that length is the underlying category of interest (following Schachter & Otanes 1972:15-18, Wolff et al. 1991:12, Zorc 1993, but contra Bloomfield 1917:141f; French 1988:63f). The penultimate syllable of native roots can bear a long vowel, as in /baːsag/ 'break' or not, as in /taŋa/ 'stupid'. Apparent final stress is thus postlexical, occurring only when the word occurs in phrase-final position. Penultimate prominence reflects a lexically specified long vowel. Long vowels can only occur in open syllables, a common state of affairs, so the paradox of heavy syllables repelling stress is illusory.
new_statements.citation: Himmelmann, Nikolaus P. & Daniel Kaufman. 2020. Austronesia. In C. Gussenhoven & A. Chen (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody, 369-383. Oxford: OUP.
new_statements.locator: Author preprint 'Prosodic systems: Austronesia' (JAN2018 draft, chapter 30, 17 pp.), §30.3 'Lexical stress', preprint pp. 5-6 (Tagalog passage, examples (1)-(2)); §30.4 Intonation, p. 10 (edge-tone association); §30.5 Prosodic integration of function words, pp. 10-11 (example (7)); §30.5 Conclusion, p. 12. Published pagination (369-383) not available.
new_statements.reading: no word stress according to the source
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: text present (the PDF's metadata: Word draft '31_Draft_Himmelmann_Kaufman_final JAN2018x.docx', A4). The quoted passage is on preprint p. 5 (extracted text, lines 46-53 of that page; lines 210-217) and matches word for word, including the parenthetical citations '(following Schachter & Otanes 1972:15-18, Wolff et al. 1991:12, Zorc 1993, but contra Bloomfield 1917:141f; French 1988:63f)' and the examples /baːsag/ and /taŋa/. Surrounding section read in full (preprint pp. 4-6): 'In Tagalog.. this prominence has alternatively been analyzed as due to underlying stress or to vowel length' (p. 5); the orthography sentence 'Both implications are probably wrong' and 'what has been analyzed as word-…
new_statements.relation_note: Placement facts agree with the existing statement (Zuraw & Roca 2025): two lexically determined classes, penult-prominent vs ultima-prominent, penult prominence shifting under suffixation. But the category differs: Himmelmann & Kaufman analyse penult prominence as lexical vowel length and final prominence as a postlexical, phrase-final edge tone, and explicitly argue against a stress analysis (contra Bloomfield 1917, French 1988), whereas Zuraw & Roca 2025 present text-setting evidence that Filipino does have word stress (their title). Different type: 'no word stress (length + edge tone)' vs 'lexical stress'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The chapter (preprint p. 5) says Tagalog roots contrast prosodic prominence on the penult vs the ultima, that 'Official Tagalog orthographic conventions.. imply that final stress is word-based.. and that penultimate stress is unmarked.. Both implications are probably wrong', and that this 'prima facie, looks like a proper stress system' but should instead be analysed as (i) a lexically specified long vowel in the (open) penult of some roots, which shifts rightward under suffixation ([ˈbaːsag] 'break' -> [baˈsaːgin]) and stays put before clitics ([baˈsaːgin mo]), and (ii) an intonation-phrase-final edge tone that lands on the final syllable of the phrase (or on the long penult if there is one: p. 10 'in Tagalog, they are regularly associated with the final syllable, unless the penultimate syllable contains a long vowel'). Closed penults never carry prominence in Tagalog (*ˈCVC.CV(C); /basbas/ -> [basˈbas]). The conclusion (p. 12) recommends 'abandoning (at least temporarily) the composite notion of word stress' for Philippine languages. So per this source Filipino/Tagalog has no word stress as such: a lexical length contrast plus phrase-level edge tones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None posited for Tagalog. The chapter notes (p. 6) that iterative trochaic stress 'has only been demonstrated for Western Malayo-Polynesian languages lacking phonemic prominence distinctions on the word level', with 'very few exceptions (e.g. French 1988, which does not contain phonetic evidence)'.
new_statements.exceptions: Length shift under suffixation (penultimate long vowel moves to the new penult); closed penult cannot be prominent (final prominence obligatory: CVC.ˈCV(C)); in phrase-medial position final prominence disappears ([aŋ ta~taŋa niˈla]); IP-final edge tone docks on the last clitic, not the host verb (b<in>ili=mo=ba, p. 10-11); roots with apparent final stress are more common than penult-stressed ones (citing Blust 2013:179), so penultimate prominence is the marked case. Loanwords with antepenultimate stress are not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 is a family-wide survey; Tagalog is discussed as the representative Philippine language (no dialect specified; elicited examples). Filipino (fili1244) is the standardized register of Tagalog (taga1270), so the statement transfers directly. The file read is the January 2018 author draft ('Prosodic systems: Austronesia', chapter 30) hosted by Universität zu Köln (KUPS record 62517) and retrieved via the the Internet Archive because the Cologne host is IPv6-only; the published 2020 text (pp. 369-383) may differ in wording and pagination, and the listed the Harvard library catalogue/ProQuest open_url is a login-gated shell.

new_statements.quote: Thus we propose the STRESS HYPOTHESIS: primary stress is contrastive in Tagalog. Both primary and secondary stress result in phonetic vowel lengthening on a nonfinal syllable. Contrastive stress is demonstrated in the following minimal pairs. (125) púno? 'trunk of a tree' / punó? 'full'; búkas 'tomorrow' / bukás 'open' ... [p. 63]. The main stress of a Tagalog stem is either ultimate or penultimate. [p. 64] ... (129) All the derivatives of a particular verb stem formed by affixation and inflection maintain the word-level stress position of the stem. ... (130) Word-level stress (ultima or penultima) of the verb stem is copied onto the corresponding syllable (ultima or penultima) after the last resyllabification. [p. 66]
new_statements.citation: French, Koleen Matsuda. 1988. Insights into Tagalog: Reduplication, Infixation, and Stress from Nonlinear Phonology. Dallas: SIL and University of Texas at Arlington, Publications in Linguistics 84.

(125) ptino? trunk of a tree / puno? full.. biikas tomorro…
new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record exists (in_catalog false); the one existing statement (Zuraw & Roca 2025: words are penult-prominent or ultima-prominent, lexically) is matched exactly by French's 'main stress of a Tagalog stem is either ultimate or penultimate' and 'primary stress is contrastive'. French adds the morphological preservation rule under affixation and a full secondary-stress system (prefix constituent, reduplicant prominence, ka- -an nouns), hence 'refines'. French does not discuss the antepenult-stressed Spanish loans that Zuraw & Roca mention as exceptions.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is lexically contrastive and falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable of the stem (minimal pairs; also noun/verb vs adjective pairs like búhay/buháy); French rejects the Schachter & Otanes vowel-length analysis in favour of contrastive stress, with stress realized as vowel lengthening on nonfinal syllables. Under suffixation the stem's penult-vs-final specification is preserved relative to the whole stem+suffix (so stress 'shifts right'), i.e. word-level stress position is a property of the stem, not of a segment.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Treated at length with a metrical-grid analysis (pp. 66-95). Prefix and stem(+suffix) are separate stress constituents, each seeking one prominent syllable; Perfect Grid alternating rhythm has almost no application in verbs. Prefix: foot-level stress on the first syllable of a polysyllabic prefix (End Rule 1), on the second if the prefix begins with ?i- (ER2), or on a heavy CVC syllable (HS); an inflected (reduplicated/infixed) prefix keeps prominence on the same relative syllable (Copy-x) unless a clash results; a reduplicated prefix syllable gets word-level prominence (e.g. makàkapag-?áral). Stem: the syllable resulting from CV-reduplication receives secondary stress (mag-?à?áral). ka- -an nouns: secondary stress on the antepenult if the stem is CVCVC, else by right-to-left Perfect Grid. Diminutive (two-syllable reduplicated) adjectives: first copy has penult secondary stress if root-initial syllable is heavy, else final. Secondary stress placement disambiguates homophones (magsàsakáh 'will farm' vs màgsasakáh 'farmer'; ka?inán verb vs kà?inán 'feast'). Monosyllabic prefixes and plural-adjective reduplicants get no secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: ka- + stem + -an derived nouns do not preserve stem stress but map predictably: bisyllabic penult-stressed stem -> final stress on the noun (báyad -> kabayarán), final-stressed bisyllabic or penult-stressed trisyllabic stem -> penultimate (tiyák -> katiyákan) (p. 82, rule 160). táwa? 'laugh' shifts to final stress under nakaka-/ka- (nakàkatawá?) (p. 84 fn.). Accepted variant forms not predicted by the rules: kapayapá?an, magsasakáh, matalitalínoh stress variants (p. 117, (223)). bigáyan/sakáyan keep penult stress because -an there is part of a derived stem, not a suffix (p. 65 fn.).
new_statements.identity_note: French 1988 describes Tagalog ('spoken natively by residents of central Luzon.. the basis for Pilipino, the national language', p. 1), with data from a Tagalog consultant and Manila-area usage including Spanish/English loans; the item fili1244 'Filipino' is the standardized national variety of Tagalog (taga1270), so the work is about this language, not a different variety.

readall_conflicts: One substantive disagreement, about the phonological category rather than placement. Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 (read in the JAN2018 author preprint) hold that Tagalog/Filipino has no word stress: the penult-vs-ultima prominence contrast reflects a lexically specified long vowel in an open penult (which shifts under suffixation) plus an intonation-phrase-final edge tone that mimics final stress only phrase-finally, and they cite Bloomfield 1917 and French 1988 as the stress-analysis camp they argue against. The existing statement in the record, Zuraw & Roca 2025, argues from text-setting evidence that Filipino does have word stress with lexically distributed penult/ultima placement (and loanword antepenults). Both sources agree on the surface facts: two lexically determined classes, penult prominence stable and mobile under suffixation, final prominence lost phrase-medially, closed penults never prominent. French 1988 could not be opened, so its own statement is unverified.

sources.note: §2.2 (pp. 3-7): the great majority of Filipino words are either penult-prominent or ultima-prominent (minimal pairs [ʔábot]/[ʔabót]); closed penults cannot bear prominence except in loans; a few loans have antepenult prominence (ʔágila); prominence shifts one syllable right under suffixation in verbs; literature split between phonemic-length and phonemic-stress analyses. §8 + §10 (pp. 20-25): text-setting evidence that both word types bear word-level stress, and that pre-tonic long/closed syllables (aspect reduplicants, closed prefixes) carry secondary stress.

sources.citation: Bloomfield, Leonard. 1917. Tagalog Texts with Grammatical Analysis. Urbana: University of Illinois (University of Illinois Studies in Language and Literature 3.2-4). Part II Phonetics, §3 Accentuation §§38-46, pp. 141-143.
sources.note: §38: at least one syllable of a polysyllable has greater stress; §39: a closed non-final syllable never has the stress, so luk-sò, ak-làt are always oxytone (exceptions: -ay syllables, mínsan, pínsan, unassimilated loans); §41-42: primary accent on a final syllable = stress + half-note pitch rise (grave), on a non-final open syllable = stress + two-note rise + vowel lengthening x1.5 (acute); §43-44: secondary accents (aspect reduplicant sùsúlat etc.) with vowel lengthening up to x2; §45-46 sentence accent, atonic words. Describes Manila Tagalog.

sources.citation: MacKinlay, W. E. W. 1905. A Handbook and Grammar of the Tagalog Language. Washington: Government Printing Office. Accents, pp. 18-19.
sources.note: 'The acute accent may fall upon any syllable, but in Tagalog is generally to be found upon the last (ultima) or the next to the last syllable (penultima)'; orthographic default: unmarked consonant-final words stressed on ultima except those in -n/-s, vowel-final on penult; suffix -an/-in draws accent one syllable rightward; 'many words are only distinguished by the accent' (asó/áso, gátas/gatás). This is the source the earlier scan used.
